en: The *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*:

Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in Rājagṛha, in the palace called the Womb of the Non-conceptual Dharmadhātu, which is preeminent throughout the entire triple world, together with a great saṃgha of bhikṣus and a great saṃgha of bodhisattvas.
Namely: by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avikalpa, by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avikalpaprabhāsa,
and by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avikalpacandra.
And by the hero of non-conceptualization;
and by the one skilled in teaching the dharma of non-conceptualization;
and by the one whose intrinsic nature is non-conceptualization.
And by Nirvikalpamati,
and by Nirvikalpanāda,
and by Nirvikalpaspharaṇa.
And with the voice of non-conceptuality; and with the voice of Maheśvara;
and with the voice of non-conceptual great loving-kindness.
Together with the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Blessed One was there indeed surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands.
He taught the Dharma,
namely, beginning with the non-conceptuality of all phenomena.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas from all sides, addressed the bodhisattvas:

“Sons of good family, you should uphold this dhāraṇī called ‘Entry into Non-conceptuality. By upholding this dhāraṇī of entry into non-conceptuality, a bodhisattva mahāsattva very swiftly accomplishes the qualities of a Buddha and proceeds toward excellence at the proper time.”

Then, in that very assembly, a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Avikalpaparabhāsa rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and, bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach the dhāraṇī called 'Entry into Non-conceptuality'."
Having heard it, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas will uphold it, recite it, and attend to it with wise reflection.
"And they shall proclaim it in detail to others.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke:
"In that case, noble sons, listen; pay close and careful attention."
"I shall speak the dhāraṇī for entering into non-conceptuality.
"Excellent, Blessed One," those bodhisattvas replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to them:

"In this regard, noble sons, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having heard the Dharma governed by non-conceptuality and having established his intention upon non-conceptuality, completely abandons all signs of conceptualization.
First of all, he completely abandons all signs of natural conceptualization."
That is to say, either the apprehended or the apprehender.
In this context, the sign of natural conceptualization is the sign within a contaminated entity.
Furthermore, a contaminated entity consists of the five aggregates of clinging.
Namely: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, and the aggregate of clinging to perception.
The aggregate of grasping at formations and the aggregate of grasping at consciousness.
Furthermore, how does one avoid those signs of conceptualization?
Through the process of appearing before the mind,
these [objects] become manifest due to the absence of mental attention (*amanasikāra*).

As he gradually abandons those signs of conceptualization, other signs of conceptualization consisting of the investigation of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) arise and become manifest through the process of appearing before the mind.
Namely: the sign of conceptualization regarding the discernment of giving; the sign of conceptualization regarding the discernment of ethical discipline;
and the sign of conceptualization regarding the discernment of patience.
The sign of conceptualization regarding the discernment of vigor;
the sign of conceptualization regarding the discernment of meditative concentration;
the sign of conceptualization regarding the discernment of wisdom.
That is to say: either by way of defining its intrinsic nature,
or by way of defining its qualities,
or by way of defining its essence.
He also avoids those signs of conceptualization that consist in the investigation of counteragents by means of non-attention.
As he avoids them, other signs of conceptualization consisting in the investigation of reality emerge and manifest for him through the process of appearing before the mind;
namely, the sign of conceptualization consisting in the investigation of emptiness.
The sign of conceptualization examining suchness;
the sign of conceptualization examining the limit of reality;
and the sign of conceptualization examining the signless ultimate realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Namely, either by way of defining its specific characteristic,
or by way of defining its qualities, or by way of defining its essence.
He also abandons those signs of conceptualization that consist in the investigation of reality by means of non-attention.
As he abandons even those, other signs of conceptualization consisting in the investigation of attainment arise and become manifest through the process of appearing to the mind.
Namely: the sign of conceptualization regarding the determination of attaining the first stage;
up to the sign of conceptualization regarding the determination of attaining the tenth stage;
and the sign of conceptualization regarding the determination of attaining the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The cause of conceptualization regarding the investigation of attaining the prophecy;
the cause of conceptualization regarding the investigation of attaining the purification of the Buddha-field;
the cause of conceptualization regarding the investigation of attaining the maturation of sentient beings.
The cause of conceptualization regarding the determination of attaining empowerment; up to the cause of conceptualization regarding the determination of attaining the knowledge of all aspects—
namely, whether by way of determining specific characteristics, or determining qualities, or determining the essence.
He also abandons those signs consisting of the conceptualization of attainment and investigation by means of non-mental engagement.
In this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, avoiding all these signs of conceptualization through non-mental engagement, becomes well-applied to non-conceptuality;
yet he does not yet touch the realm of non-conceptuality.
However, there is this fundamental concentration for the sake of touching the non-conceptual realm.

Through the sequence of cultivating that correct application, through the sequence of its frequent practice, and through the sequence of correct mental attention, he touches the non-conceptual realm either without volitional effort or effortlessly.
And he purifies them gradually.
For what reason, noble sons, is the non-conceptual realm called "non-conceptual"?
Because it transcends all conceptual examination.
By virtue of having transcended the conceptualization of teaching and seeing;
by virtue of having transcended all signs of conceptualization;
and by virtue of having transcended the conceptualization of all sense faculties.
On account of having completely transcended conceptualization regarding all objects;
on account of having completely transcended conceptualization regarding all representations;
and on account of being free from any basis for all afflictions, secondary afflictions, and obscurations to the knowable.
Therefore it is said: "The non-conceptual realm is non-conceptual.
What is that non-conceptual?
It is non-conceptual because it is formless, non-demonstrable, non-abiding, non-manifesting, non-representational, and without abode.

For the bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the non-conceptual realm perceives all phenomena as equal to space through non-conceptual gnosis that is indistinguishable from the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Through the subsequently attained gnosis, he perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, a mirror-image, the moon in water, or a magical creation.
Thereby, he attains the vastness of mastery over the dwelling in great bliss.
He attains the vastness of the great perfection of mind,
and he attains the vastness of great wisdom and knowledge.
He also attains the vastness of mastery over the dwelling in great teaching;
he becomes capable of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings at all times and in all ways,
through the unceasing and effortless performance of the Buddha’s work.
It is like this, noble sons: suppose there were a great treasure filled with various jewels beneath a mountain of solid, single-mass rock—
a treasure of radiant, diverse, and great *cintāmaṇi* gems,
such as silver or precious gems.
Or of gold and jewels;
or of emeralds and various gems.
Then, indeed, a certain person...
Suppose someone seeking a great treasure were to come along,
and a man knowledgeable about that great treasure were to say this to him:
"O man, for this single..."
Beneath this stone mountain of Maya is a great treasure-trove of radiant jewels;
beneath that is a great treasure-trove of wish-fulfilling cintāmaṇi gems.
Therefore, you should dig up nothing but the natural rock itself.
As you dig there, a stone appearing like silver will come into view;
even regarding that, you must not form the notion that it is a great treasure.
Having thoroughly understood that, it should be excavated.
As you excavate it, a stone appearing like gold will come into view.
Even in that case, you should not form the notion that it is a great treasure.
Having fully understood that as well, it must be excavated.
As you are excavating it, a stone appearing like various jewels will come into view.
Even in that case, you should not form the notion that it is a great treasure;
having recognized it as such, it too must be dug up.

"In this way, O man, being well-applied, you shall see that great treasure-store of the wish-fulfilling jewel (mahācintāmaṇiratnanidhāna), which has been dug up, without any further effort or exertion.

And by obtaining that great treasure-store of jewels, you will become wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, and you will be capable of fulfilling the aims of both yourself and others."
For indeed, noble sons, this simile has been made solely for the purpose of making this matter known.
"A mountain of solid rock consisting of a single mass of essence" is a designation for the various types of conditioned phenomena that arise from the presence of the two kinds of affliction.
"Below lies a treasure-trove of great wish-fulfilling jewels"—this is a designation for the realm free from conceptual construction (*avikalpadhātu*).
"One who seeks the treasure-trove of great wish-fulfilling jewels"—this is a designation for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
"A person possessing the super-knowledge of the great jewel-treasure"—this is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) is a designation for the signs of conceptualizing nature, such as "stone";
"digging up" is a designation for non-mental engagement (*amanasikāra*).

"A stone appearing as silver" is a designation for the signs of conceptualization that discerns counteragents; "a stone appearing as gold" is a designation for the signs of conceptualization regarding emptiness and so forth;
[and] "appearing as various jewels"...
"Stone" is a designation for the signs of conceptualization regarding attainment;
"the acquisition of a great treasure of wish-fulfilling jewels" is a designation for the touching of the non-conceptual realm.
Thus, noble sons, by means of this introduction of a simile, the entry into non-conceptuality is to be understood.
Furthermore, noble sons, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while examining these aforementioned signs of conceptualization, enter the realm of non-conceptualization?
Here, noble sons, a bodhisattva mahāsattva established in the realm of non-conceptualization, when the sign of conceptualizing the intrinsic nature of form appears before him, examines it thus:
"He who courses with the thought 'this is my form' courses in conceptualization."
To practice with the thought "this is the form of others" is to practice in conceptualization; to practice with the thought "this is form" is to practice in conceptualization;
[to think] "form arises" [is to practice in conceptualization].
It ceases;
it becomes afflicted; it is purified—thus one practices.
Thus one courses in conceptual construction;
to course with the thought "form does not exist" is to course in conceptual construction;
it does not exist even by way of intrinsic nature.
It does not exist even as a cause;
it does not exist even as a result;
it does not exist even as an action.

To practice with the thought that "form does not exist by way of yoga, nor does it exist by way of manifestation" is to practice in conceptual construction. To practice with the thought that "form is representation-only" is to practice in conceptual construction.
Just as form does not exist, so too representation appearing as form does not exist.
Thus he courses; he courses in conceptual construction.
And because, noble son, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not apprehend "form," nor does he apprehend even the representation that appears as form.
Nor does he cause representation to perish entirely in every respect;
nor does he perceive anything other than representation as being non-existent,
nor does he perceive non-existence as being other than representation.
And he does not perceive the non-existence of that representation appearing as form as being identical with that representation,
nor does he perceive it as different from it;
nor does he perceive the non-existence of the representation as a real entity.
He does not perceive it as non-existent.
Noble sons,
he who does not conceptualize by means of any modes or any conceptual constructions does not perceive this as "the realm of non-conceptuality."
"O sons of good family, this is the method of entry into the non-conceptual realm;
and in this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in the non-conceptual realm."
In the same way [it is for] feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

likewise for the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
In this way, [the analysis] of emptiness and so forth should be applied up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Here, sons of good family, when the signs of conceptualization that define the knowledge of all aspects have appeared before him, a bodhisattva mahāsattva investigates thus:
"He who practices with the thought 'this is my knowledge of all aspects' is practicing in conceptualization."
If he practices thinking, "This is the omniscience of all aspects for those others," he practices in conceptualization;
if he practices thinking, "This is omniscience of all aspects," he practices in conceptualization;
if he practices thinking, "Omniscience of all aspects is attained," he practices in conceptualization.

To practice with the thought that "the knowledge of all aspects is for the sake of abandoning all afflictions and the obstructions to the knowable" is to practice in conceptualization. To practice with the thought that "there is no triple world other than the purification of the knowledge of all aspects" is to practice in conceptualization.
[The notion] that "the knowledge of all aspects arises" [is likewise].
To think that "it ceases," "it becomes defiled," or "it becomes purified" is to course in conceptual construction;
one courses in conceptual construction.
To think that "all-aspect omniscience does not exist" is to course in conceptualization;
it does not exist even by way of intrinsic nature.
It does not exist from the perspective of its cause; it does not exist from the perspective of its fruit; it does not exist from the perspective of its action.

To practice with the thought that "even from the perspective of yoga it does not exist" or "even from the perspective of its occurrence it does not exist" is to practice in conceptualization; to practice with the thought that "all-aspect omniscience is representation-only" is to practice in conceptualization.
Just as omniscience does not exist, so too the representation that is the appearance of omniscience does not exist; to practice in this way is to practice in conceptual construction.
And because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive omniscience in any way whatsoever, [he does not practice in conceptual construction].
In that very same way, he does not perceive even the representation appearing as that;
nor does he completely destroy that representation;
nor does he perceive any dharma other than that representation.
He does not perceive that representation as having non-existence,
nor does he perceive non-existence apart from the representation.
Nor does he perceive the non-existence of that representation as being identical with that representation,
nor does he perceive it as being separate from it.
Furthermore, he does not perceive the non-existence of that representation as being existent,

nor does he perceive it as being non-existent. Sons of good family, he who does not conceptualize through any mode or any conceptualization, and who does not perceive [it] as "this is the non-conceptual realm of phenomena" (avikalpa-dharmadhātu)— [he is one who dwells therein].
Such is this method of entry into the non-conceptual realm.
For in this way, noble sons, a bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in the non-conceptual realm.

Noble sons, the merit derived from the grasping, writing, and reciting of this Dharma discourse is far greater than that of sacrificing bodies as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, or even that of giving gifts of jewels filling world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
"Is it not so that this mass of merit from having caused images of the Tathāgata to be made, filling as many world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, [surpasses the former]?
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
Having become one whose disposition is free from conceptual construction regarding this True Dharma, the Son of the Victor,
having transcended the difficult terrain of conceptualization, gradually attains the state that is non-conceptual,
peaceful, immovable, supreme, and under control. (1)
Because it is equal to the ultimate, the Bodhisattva thereby attains non-conceptual bliss. (2)
The Blessed One said this, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avikalpaprabhāsa, with a joyful mind, as well as that entire assembly and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas,
rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
